## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a04-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Cost of service</dt><dd>What serving a customer costs in this model: energy each hour, plants for the town's tightest hour (most gas needed), local wires for its own busiest hour, and a meter.</dd>
<dt>A tariff</dt><dd>The rule that turns those costs into a bill: a fixed charge, prices per kWh, and charges per kW.</dd>
<dt>Revenue-neutral</dt><dd>Each tariff is set so that a class of customers pays its total cost before anyone changes what they do.</dd>
<dt>Cross-subsidy</dt><dd>When one customer pays above its cost so another can pay below it, inside the same class.</dd>
<dt>What a tariff rewards</dt><dd>A move pays off on the bill only if the tariff charges for what the move changes.</dd>
<dt>Large-load tariff</dt><dd>Minimum bills, long contracts and exit fees can reduce other customers' exposure to a large load's upgrades; how much depends on their amounts and terms.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Setting prices so that a class pays its cost</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The homes' class is nine renters and one solar and EV home. Serving them costs $897.58 a month, and they use 5,416.7 kWh net.

| Tariff | How its price is set | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Flat | ($897.58 − 10 × $10 fixed) ÷ 5,416.7 kWh | 14.7¢ per kWh |
| Time-of-use | the same $797.58 ÷ (3,233.6 off-peak kWh + 3 × 2,183.2 peak kWh) | 8.2¢ off-peak, 24.5¢ peak |
| Demand charge | plants and wires, $515.59, ÷ the sum of the busiest hours, 24.55 kW | $21.00 per kW, plus 5.2¢ per kWh for energy |
| Real-time | plants and wires, $515.59, ÷ 5,416.7 kWh | a plant-and-wire charge of 9.5¢ per kWh on top of each hour's price |

- **Revenue-neutral.** Every row collects the same $897.58 at the start; they differ in who pays it.
- **Real [rate cases]{.lx-term term="rate-case"}**, the regulator's reviews that set a utility's prices, add more classes, many hours instead of one tightest hour, and a year of weather.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Net metering, net billing and what a kWh sent back is worth</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **[Net metering]{.lx-term term="net-metering"}.** A kWh sent back earns what a kWh bought costs: 14.7¢ under the flat price.
- **What it is worth.** At midday on 9 June the town is spilling sun, so one more kWh is worth $0 to it.
- **[Net billing]{.lx-term term="net-billing"}.** Credit each kWh sent back at the hour's running cost, and re-set the flat price so homes still pay their cost: it falls to 13.5¢.
- **The result.** The renter's bill falls from $92 to $86; the solar and EV home's rises from $66 to $127, still below its $262 cost.
- **Why still below.** Its car charges in the tightest hour, and kWh prices do not see kW.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>A bill as a function of 24 hourly loads</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Write the customer's net load in hour $t$ as $x_t$ (kW, held for the hour), $\Delta t$ = 1 hour and $n$ = 30 days. Every tariff in this lesson is

$$\text{bill}(x) = F + n \sum_{t} p_t\, x_t\, \Delta t + d \max_t x_t$$

- $F$ is the fixed charge ($ a month), $p_t$ the price of a kWh in hour $t$ ($ per kWh) and $d$ the demand charge ($ per kW).
- **Power and energy.** $x_t\,\Delta t$ is energy: one kW held for one hour uses one kWh, so $p_t\, x_t\, \Delta t$ is in dollars.
- **What it rewards.** One kW less in hour $t$ cuts the bill by $n p_t\,\Delta t$. The demand charge falls only when the highest hourly demand falls: all tied peaks must come down (the factory's 13:00 and 14:00).
- **What it should reward.** The cost of service has the same shape, with the town's price in $p_t$, plants on the tightest hour's $x_t$ and wires on $\max_t x_t$.
- **Cost-reflective.** A tariff whose slopes (how the bill changes when one hour's kW changes) match the cost's slopes sends the right signals for the costs this model represents; each of the four matches only part.
- **Next.** City models with screening fairness outputs come in [M12](m12-city-model.html); who pays and who benefits in [A13](a13-fairness-jobs.html); flexible demand in [A7](a07-flexible-demand.html).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a04-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="flat" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “One flat price per kWh charges every customer for the costs it causes.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the toy the renter pays $22 above its cost and the solar and EV home $196 below: kWh are not what drives plants and wires.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="demand" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A demand charge rewards exactly what lowers the grid's costs.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Moving the factory's batch saves $3,000 on its bill, but the model's cost of serving it falls only $720: the charge sees the factory's own peak, not the town's tightest hour.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="risk" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Real-time pricing puts the risk of price spikes on the customer.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact: a scarcity week raises the renter's real-time bill from $88 to $132. Under the other tariffs the utility pays first; here we assume it recovers that from all customers later.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="min" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A minimum bill can protect other customers when a large load's demand stays below its contract.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. With its highest demand at half its contract, other customers pay $7.5M a year of the upgrades with no minimum, and $3.0M with a minimum of 80% (if they cover what it does not pay).</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a04">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="ev" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Without the scarcity week, under which tariff does moving the car's charging from 19:00 to 01:00 save its owner the most?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Flat</li><li data-value="b">Time-of-use</li><li data-value="c">Demand charge</li><li data-value="d">Real-time</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Time-of-use: $68 a month, against $30 under the demand charge, $13 under real-time and nothing flat; the model's cost of serving the home falls $126. With the scarcity week on, real-time saves $79, time-of-use still $68.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card a4-practice">

Prices were set so the class pays its cost.</p></details></li><li><p><b>A lower busiest hour for the factory.</b></p><p>Its demand charge is $15 per kW; moving the batch cuts its busiest hour by 200 kW. Is 16:00 to 21:00 a good window?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Only partly: at 16:00 sun is still spare (the town's price is $0), and 21:00 to 23:00 is left out.
